title: MLB Pitching Workload 2026
text:
The question
Major League Baseball front offices, pitching coaches, and player development staff invest heavily in pitcher health and in-game bullpen management, making it critical to distinguish genuine physical fatigue from simple pitch-count heuristics. This case study asks: How effectively do a starting pitcher’s workload (pitch count) and command (walks and strikeouts), after controlling for average velocity and spin rate, predict runs allowed per start in September 2025?
To answer this question, we aggregated pitch-level MLB Advanced Media (Statcast) tracking data from the September 2025 regular season using the baseballr R package. Each observational unit is an individual starting pitcher appearance (\(n = 246\) starts), with total runs allowed (runs_allowed) as the response variable and five key predictors: pitch_count, walks, strikeouts, avg_velocity, and avg_spin_rate. A central data limitation is managerial selection bias (survival bias): because managers pull struggling pitchers early, higher pitch counts appear artificially linked to fewer runs allowed unless command and pitch quality are accounted for.

title: MLB Pitching Workload 2026
text:
What the baseline shows
Describe and justify a simple course-based baseline regression model. Interpret the result that best establishes the rest of the story, including its direction, magnitude, scale, and uncertainty. Explain one limitation or unresolved pattern that motivates deeper analysis. We fit a simple linear regression (SLR) predicting runs allowed per start from pitch count alone (\(\text{runs\_allowed}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{pitch\_count}_i + \epsilon_i\)). This baseline directly tests the naive assumption that heavier in-game workloads correspond to more runs allowed.
Contrary to that intuition, the fitted slope is negative and statistically significant (\(\hat{\beta}_1 = -0.019\), \(p = 0.007\)), meaning every additional 10 pitches thrown is associated with roughly 0.19 fewer runs allowed on average. Still, pitch count alone explains less than 3% of the variance in scoring (\(R^2 = 0.0294\)), leaving wide uncertainty around individual outings. This counterintuitive negative trend reflects managerial selection bias rather than a protective effect of fatigue: pitchers who surrender runs early are pulled quickly, while effective pitchers earn deeper outings. Isolating true workload effects requires controlling for command and pitch quality.


Show code
# Load packages and data, document preparation, and fit the baseline.
library(baseballr)
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

# 1. Pull September 2025 Statcast data
statcast_raw <- scrape_statcast_savant(
  start_date = "2025-09-01",
  end_date = "2025-09-30",
  player_type = "pitcher"
)

# 2. Aggregate to starting pitcher appearances (fixing runs_allowed by inning half)
starting_pitcher_data <- statcast_raw %>%
  mutate(
    runs_on_pitch = if_else(
      inning_topbot == "Top",
      post_away_score - away_score,
      post_home_score - home_score
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(game_pk, game_date, pitcher, player_name) %>%
  summarise(
    pitch_count = n(),
    strikeouts = sum(events == "strikeout", na.rm = TRUE),
    walks = sum(events == "walk", na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_velocity = mean(release_speed, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_spin_rate = mean(release_spin_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    runs_allowed = sum(runs_on_pitch, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(pitch_count >= 30)

# 3. Fit baseline SLR
baseline_mod <- lm(runs_allowed ~ pitch_count, data = starting_pitcher_data)

tidy(baseline_mod, conf.int = TRUE)

Going beyond the baseline

Do nonlinear workload and pitch-quality interactions explain performance degradation?
To capture the curved baseline trend, we fit a multiple linear regression adding command (walks, strikeouts), pitch quality (avg_velocity, avg_spin_rate), \(\text{pitch\_count}^2\), and workload-by-stuff interactions. A nested F-test confirms a significant improvement over the baseline (\(F = [\text{value}]\), \(p = [\text{value}]\); adjusted \(R^2\) rises from \([\text{base } R^2]\) to \([\text{new } R^2]\)). Walks increase expected runs (\(\hat{\beta}_{\text{walks}} = [\text{value}]\)) while strikeouts reduce them (\(\hat{\beta}_{\text{SO}} = [\text{value}]\)), but high VIFs among the polynomial and interaction terms motivate regularization next.


Show code
# Analysis code for this part.
library(car)

m_poly_int <- lm(
  runs_allowed ~ poly(pitch_count, 2, raw = TRUE) + walks + strikeouts +
    avg_velocity + avg_spin_rate +
    pitch_count:avg_velocity + pitch_count:avg_spin_rate,
  data = starting_pitcher_data
)

# Nested F-test vs. baseline, coefficients, and fit metrics
anova(baseline_mod, m_poly_int)

Which predictors survive Ridge, Elastic Net, and LASSO regularization?
To address multicollinearity among pitch metrics and prevent overfitting, we compared three 10-fold cross-validated regularized models across the same predictors: Ridge (\(\alpha = 0\)), Elastic Net (\(\alpha = 0.5\)), and LASSO (\(\alpha = 1\)). Ridge shrinks correlated predictors together, LASSO performs variable selection by zeroing out weak terms, and Elastic Net balances both.Across 10-fold cross-validation, \([\text{best model}]\) achieves the lowest out-of-sample RMSE at \([\text{value}]\) runs (Table 1). At the parsimonious lambda.1se penalty, LASSO retains \([\text{retained predictors}]\) while shrinking \([\text{zeroed predictors}]\) to zero. This reinforces that in-game command (walks and strikeouts) and workload structure drive run prevention far more reliably than raw average velocity or spin rate alone.


Show code
# Analysis code for this part.
library(glmnet)
library(knitr)

set.seed(330)
X <- model.matrix(
  runs_allowed ~ poly(pitch_count, 2, raw = TRUE) + walks + strikeouts +
    avg_velocity + avg_spin_rate +
    pitch_count:avg_velocity + pitch_count:avg_spin_rate,
  data = starting_pitcher_data
)[, -1]
y <- starting_pitcher_data$runs_allowed

# Use identical CV folds across all three models for a fair comparison
foldid <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = length(y)))

cv_ridge <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0,   foldid = foldid)
cv_enet  <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5, foldid = foldid)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 1,   foldid = foldid)

# Summary comparison table (counts as Visual 2 of your 4-visual limit)
reg_summary <- tibble(
  Model = c("Ridge (alpha = 0)", "Elastic Net (alpha = 0.5)", "LASSO (alpha = 1)"),
  `CV RMSE (lambda.min)` = round(c(sqrt(min(cv_ridge$cvm)), sqrt(min(cv_enet$cvm)), sqrt(min(cv_lasso$cvm))), 3),
  `CV RMSE (lambda.1se)` = round(c(
    sqrt(cv_ridge$cvm[cv_ridge$lambda == cv_ridge$lambda.1se]),
    sqrt(cv_enet$cvm[cv_enet$lambda == cv_enet$lambda.1se]),
    sqrt(cv_lasso$cvm[cv_lasso$lambda == cv_lasso$lambda.1se])
  ), 3),
  `Non-zero predictors (1se)` = c(
    sum(coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.1se")[-1] != 0),
    sum(coef(cv_enet,  s = "lambda.1se")[-1] != 0),
    sum(coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")[-1] != 0)
  )
)
